Now I have a clearer picture of the editorial landscape:

Supporting YES:
- SPUR (Vote YES)
- McClatchy California editorial boards (Sacramento Bee, Fresno Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, San Luis Obispo Tribune) - strongly endorsed yes
- George Skelton (LA Times columnist) - Yes
- Mark Z. Barabak (LA Times columnist) - supportive commentary
- League of Women Voters of California
- California Common Cause
- Secretary of State Shirley Weber
- Lt. Gov. Eleni Kounalakis
- California Democratic Party
- California Labor Federation
- Indivisible CA: StateStrong

Supporting NO:
- SF Chronicle editorial board (because of the provision letting recalled officials run in the replacement special election)
- Southern California News Group (SCNG) / Press-Telegram / OC Register / Daily News (Los Angeles Daily News) - No
- San Diego Union-Tribune - No
- Santa Cruz Sentinel / Bay Area News Group - No
- California Republican Party
- Election Integrity Project California
- Senate Minority Leader Brian W. Jones, Assemblymember Joe Patterson

Polling: PPIC September poll found 59% of likely voters would vote against, 35% for.

Key substance:
- The measure eliminates the two-question recall ballot. Currently, a replacement can win with a tiny plurality (2003: Schwarzenegger 48.6%; 2021: Larry Elder would have needed only ~28% of voters' support). 
- Under Prop 5, Governor recalled → Lt. Governor takes over (until next statewide election if early in term, else for remainder). Lt. Gov is statewide elected, so has democratic legitimacy.
- Other statewide officials → Governor appoints (same as vacancy rules for resignation/death)
- Legislators → special election (same as vacancy rules)
- Recalled official may run in the special election (this reverses current ban)
- Fiscal effect: unknown, could be savings or costs of millions

Arguments for yes:
1. Majority rule: prevents someone becoming governor with ~28% of voter support while the recalled official got 49%+ — an undemocratic outcome.
2. Reduces incentive for partisan recall attempts as a "second bite at the apple" — currently the minority party can use recalls strategically.
3. Aligns California with most states (only 6 other states use two-question ballots); aligns recall vacancies with normal vacancy rules.
4. Cleaner ballots, less confusion.
5. Keeps the recall itself fully intact — voters still retain the power to remove an official.
6. Supported by good-government groups (LWV, Common Cause).

Arguments for no:
1. Takes away voters' immediate right to choose a replacement; hands power to the Governor (appointments) — "political insiders."
2. For legislative seats, vacancies of months and another costly special election.
3. Recalled official can run in the special election to replace themselves — bizarre provision that even the author couldn't justify. This could produce absurd outcomes: official recalled, then re-elected months later in a special election, but meanwhile the office was vacant and taxpayers paid for two elections.
4. Motivated by incumbent protection ("Newman's Revenge") — the author was recalled in 2018.
5. Lt. Gov automatically becoming Governor may not reflect the will of the voters seeking change.

Now, what's the best recommendation? The user asks "Is it better to vote yes or no on this prop?" and wants me to answer with only "yes" or "no."

Let me weigh the evidence:

The merits: The core reform (removing the second question) is well-supported by good-government logic and political science. The current system allows a replacement to win with a small plurality while a majority may have voted against recall. In 2021, Larry Elder could have become governor with the support of ~28% of recall voters. That's a genuinely undemocratic outcome. Also, the two-question setup creates perverse incentives — it encourages recalls as partisan power grabs, and it can also cause voters to keep an unpopular official because they fear the replacement (e.g., 2003 Davis vs. Schwarzenegger dynamics; 2021 Newsom).

Most states with recalls don't do same-day successor elections. California's system is anomalous. Aligning recall vacancies with existing vacancy procedures is coherent: if an official dies or resigns, the Lt. Gov takes over or the Governor appoints or a special election is held. The recall question should simply be about removal.

The recall power itself is preserved — voters retain the ability to remove an official by majority vote. That's the core accountability tool.

The flaw: the provision allowing recalled officials to run in the special election to fill their own seat. The SF Chronicle opposes the measure primarily because of this. But is this really disqualifying? Under current law, a recalled official cannot be a candidate in the same recall's replacement election, but they can run in the NEXT regular election (as Newman did in 2020, winning his seat back). The Prop 5 provision simply extends that right to the special election to fill the vacancy. One could argue it's democratic — the voters can decide; if they really want the official back, they can vote them back in, but now in a head-to-head contest (well, a plurality contest among special election candidates, actually still plurality). Hmm, but the special election to fill a vacancy is itself a plurality-winner election... So a recalled official could win the special election with, say, 30% of the vote. That does undermine the "majority rule" argument somewhat.

But note: the same is true today. The recalled official can run at the next regular election. The measure doesn't create incumbency advantage per se; it preserves the voters' right to choose, which is the very thing opponents say they want. Actually, opponents argue both sides: (1) it takes away voters' right to choose the replacement, AND (2) it lets the recalled official run again. These are somewhat in tension — allowing the recalled official to run in the special election actually gives voters MORE choice, not less. The Chronicle's complaint is more about the unlimited recall campaign funds incumbents can raise, which is a fair concern.

Weighing everything: 

The good-government community (LWV, Common Cause, SPUR, McClatchy editorial boards, Skelton, Barabak, Secretary of State Weber) supports it. The opposition is largely partisan-Republican (CA GOP, SCNG papers, SDUT, SF Chronicle on a narrower ground). 

The strongest substantive case for NO is:
1. Governor appointments for statewide officials reduce voter choice.
2. Extra special elections cost money and leave districts unrepresented for months.
3. The recalled-official-can-run-again provision.

The strongest substantive case for YES is:
1. Majority rule — prevents 28%-support governors.
2. Prevents recalls from being weaponized as partisan do-overs.
3. Consistency with vacancy rules and other states.
4. Preserves the recall power itself.

On balance, I think the merits favor YES. The core problem Prop 5 addresses is real and well-documented: the 2021 recall nearly installed a governor with 28% support after a $200M+ election; the 2003 recall was driven partly by the successor question. The reform keeps the recall fully intact while fixing the plurality-loophole. The criticisms are largely secondary (cost of special elections is modest and rare; the recalled-official provision is a flaw but a marginal one that preserves voter choice — and voters can reject that official).

Also worth noting: polling shows it's likely to fail (59% opposed in PPIC), but the question is what's better, not what will pass.

Let me also consider the concern that this is "incumbent protection." Both parties would be affected equally in principle. Recalls are rarely used (11 qualified since 1913, 6 successful). The measure's effect on minority-party strategy is real but that's the point: recalls shouldn't be a tool for the minority party to seize offices via plurality races outside the regular cycle. If an official is truly unfit, a majority will still remove them, and the vacancy will be filled under normal rules.

One more consideration: the concern that "voters won't vote yes on recall because they won't get to choose the replacement" — some argue this makes recalls less likely to succeed, making incumbents safer. Counter: if voters genuinely want the official gone, they'll vote them out. The replacement question has actually distorted recall voting in the other direction — voters who oppose the official might vote NO on recall because they fear the replacement (this was a documented dynamic in 2003 and 2021). Removing question 2 focuses the vote on the official's fitness.

Also, importantly: the Lt. Gov is independently elected statewide, so succession to Governor maintains democratic legitimacy (similar to the U.S. presidential succession). And if the recall happens early in the term, voters elect a new Governor at the next statewide election anyway.

I'm fairly convinced the balance of arguments and expert opinion favors YES. Let me do a bit more research to make sure I'm not missing anything major — let me check the McClatchy/Sacramento Bee endorsement reasoning and any other good-government analyses, and maybe the PPIC poll details. Also let me verify the NCSL data about other states.

Actually, let me look at the Sacramento Bee endorsement article and the IGS Berkeley guide for a balanced summary. Let me also quickly check the LA Times' formal editorial board position if they have one.

Proposition 5 : Change how recalled state officials are replaced
Published September 29, 2026 · Updated November 2, 2026
Proposition 5 would remove the second question from state recall elections, the one asking who should replace the official if recalled. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor, either for the rest of the term or until voters elect a new Governor, depending on timing. Other recalled offices would be filled the way vacancies are filled now: a special election for legislators and appointment by the Governor for most other offices.
Summary by CityHallPass , not the official text or legal advice. The official text controls: California Official Voter Information Guide: Proposition 5 (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/).

What does a yes vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
What does a no vote on Proposition 5 mean?
Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
What would Proposition 5 cost?
The Legislative Analyst says the net effect is unknown. Separate special elections could cost millions of dollars each, while dropping replacement candidates from recall ballots could save millions. The Analyst says these costs or savings would be rare and depend on which office is recalled.
What it means for the City of LA
Proposition 5 covers only state officers: the Governor, other statewide officials, legislators and certain judges. Recalls of the Mayor, City Council members and other City officials follow the City Charter, which puts the recall question and the election of a successor on the same ballot; Proposition 5 does not change that. City residents would still vote in any state recall, and Los Angeles County's cost for the 2021 Governor recall was $52.9 million.
The details
Official title Changes Recall Election Process for Statewide Officers. Legislative Constitutional Amendment.
Type Legislative constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by the Legislature (SCA 1, Resolution Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024)
Votes needed to pass Simple majority (more than 50% yes) of votes cast statewide. Under the State Constitution (Article XVIII, Section 4), an amendment takes effect if "approved by a majority of votes cast thereon."
The question on your ballot
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
This is not the Proposition 5 on the November 5, 2024 ballot, the measure on local bonds for affordable housing and infrastructure, which failed with 45.0% voting yes (Secretary of State, November 2024 Statement of Vote (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2024-general/sov/59-state-ballot-measures.pdf)).
What would change
Today If Proposition 5 passes
Recall ballot Two questions: remove the official, and who replaces them if removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) One question: remove the official or not (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Who takes office after a recall The replacement candidate with the most votes, even without a majority (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)) The office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules (text, Art. II, Sec. 15(c) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled Governor Replaced by the top replacement candidate The Lieutenant Governor becomes Governor. If the recall comes before the nomination period closes for the next statewide election in the first two years of the term, a special election is held with the next statewide primary, and a runoff at the general election if no one gets a majority. Otherwise the Lieutenant Governor serves out the term (text, Art. V, Sec. 10(b) (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
Recalled legislator Replaced by the top replacement candidate Seat filled by a special election called by the Governor (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Other recalled state officers (e.g. Attorney General) Replaced by the top replacement candidate Governor appoints a replacement under existing vacancy rules (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm))
Can the recalled official run again? May not be a candidate to replace themselves (text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)) May run in the later special election, but may not be appointed to the seat (title and summary (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/title-summary.htm); text (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf))
The rules for qualifying a recall, such as signature counts and deadlines, do not change. A recall election must still be held 60 to 80 days after signatures are certified, or within 180 days if combined with a regular election (text, Art. II, Sec. 15 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf)).
What it means for the City of Los Angeles
City recalls are not affected. Proposition 5 amends only Sections 15 and 17 of Article II and Section 10 of Article V of the State Constitution, which cover state officers (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)). Recalls of City officials follow the City Charter. When a City recall petition qualifies, the Council calls an election on whether to recall the officer “and if recalled, for the election of his or her successor” (City Clerk petition handbook, p. 21, citing Charter sec. 432 (https://clerk.lacity.gov/sites/g/files/wph1491/files/2021-03/lacityp_023253.pdf#page=21)). That two-part City process stays the same.
City voters and state recalls. City residents vote in any statewide recall and in recalls of legislators who represent them. In the 2021 Governor recall, Los Angeles County voters opposed removal 70.8% to 29.2% (Statement of Vote, recall question (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/16-question.pdf)).
Election costs. County election offices run state recalls. Los Angeles County reported $52,920,735 in costs for the 2021 recall, against a state allocation of $59,793,000 (Secretary of State cost report (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/statewide-elections/2021-recall/report-to-legislature.pdf)). The Analyst says Proposition 5 could raise or lower future recall costs and that the split between the state and counties “would depend on future decisions by the Legislature” (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm)).
We found no City Council or City Clerk position on Proposition 5 as of Sept. 30, 2026.
How it got on the ballot
A constitutional amendment written by the Legislature needs a two-thirds vote of each house (SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Jan. 30, 2023: Sen. Josh Newman introduced SCA 1. Assemblymember Isaac Bryan was the principal coauthor (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1); SCA 1 status (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Feb. 1, 2024: The Senate adopted it 31-7 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)).
Aug. 30-31, 2024: The Assembly adopted the amended version 59-17 and the Senate agreed 32-8 (SCA 1 votes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). The Senate no votes were Alvarado-Gil, Dahle, Grove, Jones, Nguyen, Niello, Ochoa Bogh and Seyarto.
Sept. 10, 2024: Filed with the Secretary of State as Resolution Chapter 204 (SCA 1 history (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billHistoryClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1)). It appears on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot (SOS voter guide (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/)).
The 2018 recall of the measure’s author. Newman was recalled from the 29th Senate District in 2018, and Republican Ling Ling Chang was elected his successor on the same ballot (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). The Daily News reports the recall passed 58% to 42% after Newman voted for a gas tax increase in 2017, and that he won the seat back in 2020 (Daily News (https://www.dailynews.com/2026/08/12/endorsement-vote-no-on-proposition-5-an-attack-on-californias-recall-power/)). The Sacramento Bee reports Chang won with just under 34% of the vote (Sacramento Bee via MSN (https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/other/proposition-5-could-change-california-s-recall-elections-here-is-our-endorsement-opinion/ar-AA2cxbHa)).
Why the vote threshold is a simple majority. A constitutional amendment “if approved by a majority of votes cast thereon, takes effect” (Cal. Const. art. XVIII, sec. 4 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CONS&sectionNum=SEC.%204.&article=XVIII)).
Recall history. Since 1913, 11 state recalls have qualified for the ballot, nine against legislators and two against Governors, and six officials were removed (LAO analysis (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/5/analysis.htm); Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)). Two of the qualified recalls, both in 1994, targeted Los Angeles County legislators: Sen. David Roberti, who kept his seat, and Assemblyman Paul Horcher, who was removed (Secretary of State recall history (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/sov/2021-recall/sov/06-ca-recall-history.pdf)).

Proposition 5
Delay replacing recalled state officials
Under current law, after choosing whether to recall an elected official, voters are asked who should replace them. This constitutional amendment, placed on the ballot by state lawmakers, would delay the election of a successor until a separate election. The recalled officer would be allowed to run in that election. If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would take over their duties until a new governor is elected. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

Summary
Support
Proposition 5 is a constitutional amendment born out of a proposal from the secretary of state’s office following the unsuccessful recall of Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. Secretary of State Shirley Weber told lawmakers her office felt a recall election should focus on whether the elected official should be recalled, not whether other potential candidates would be better in the role. Democrat Josh Newman, who was successfully recalled from his state Senate seat in 2018, authored the measure, saying it would reduce the “political gamesmanship” that elevates candidates who otherwise wouldn’t receive a majority of votes.
Oppose
Opponents including the California Republican Party and Election Integrity Project, which advocates for voter ID requirements and restrictions on mail-in voting, argue that allowing the lieutenant governor to assume the governor’s position if the governor were recalled would dissuade people from participating in a recall election. Almost all legislative Republicans also opposed it, arguing that it would dilute the power of voters while protecting incumbents. The current recall process is how former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, a Republican, was first elected in 2003.

# Should California’s state politician recall elections change? Prop. 5 explained
*Proposition 5 amends California’s Constitution to change how recall elections work, severing the recall vote from who replaces the official in office.
Below is a transcript of the video above.
Read our voter guide story on Prop.
5 here, along with the editorial board’s take on the issue.*
How a politician gets kicked out of office in California — and who takes their spot — could soon change.
Right now, when there’s a recall election, you answer two questions at once.
Should this politician go?
And who should replace them?
Proposition 5 drops that second question.
So if the governor got recalled, the lieutenant governor would step in.
Here’s why it matters.
Back in 2021, Gavin Newsom survived his recall.
But if he hadn’t, Larry Elder would’ve taken over — with just 28% of the vote.
There have been 182 recall attempts of state elected officials.
Only 11 actually qualified for the ballot, and the elected official was only removed six times.
Former state Senator Josh Newman wrote the measure.
He is one of the six in California history who was removed from office.
He says it makes sure whoever wins actually has a broad base of support.
Opponents, including top California Republicans, say it protects the party in power and limits voter choice.
A yes vote changes the rules.
A no vote keeps them the same.
It’s your call on Nov. 3.

For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

Proposition 5 could change California’s recall elections. Here is our endorsement | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated October 5, 2026 8:16 AM
Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html) seeks to fundamentally change how California conducts recall elections for members of the Legislature and constitutional officers elected statewide. Such elections have been rare in California.
According to theLegislative Analyst’s Office, (https://lao.ca.gov/) only 11 state recall efforts targeting nine legislators and two governors have qualified for the ballot since 1913. In 2003, Gray Davis (https://www.modbee.com/opinion/opn-columns-blogs/article251385288.html) became the only California governor to be recalled, a fate that also befell five state legislators over the years. The last statewide recall effort to qualify for the ballot was the unsuccessful campaign to oust Gov. Gavin Newsom in 2021. (https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/editorials/article253266413.html)
Under current law, voters are asked two questions in the same election when a recall effort qualifies for the ballot. The first is whether a state officer should be recalled. The second is who should replace that officer from a field of hopefuls seeking consideration if a recall is successful. In 2003, 135 candidates wanted to succeed Davis. In 2021, there were 46 candidates vying for Newsom’s job.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 5 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/election/voter-guide/article317117877.html)
If Prop. 5 is approved by state voters in November, the second question will be eliminated.
In future statewide recalls that gather enough signatures to qualify for the ballot, Californians would only vote yes or no on whether an officer should be recalled. If a state recall of a member of the Legislature was successful, that office would remain vacant until a special election was held. If a constitutional officer were recalled, the vacancies would be filled by the governor. Should a future governor be recalled in the first two years of office, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until a special election was held. If a governor were recalled later in the term, the Lt. Gov. would fill the vacancy until the next scheduled election.
This would be a longer process, but also one that’s more thoughtful, deliberate and — most importantly — respects the democratic norm of majority rule.
It’s why our combined editorial boards representing The Sacramento Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, Fresno Bee and San Luis Obispo Tribune endorse Prop. 5.
Recall elections in California
Since California voters approved the recall process in 1911, five replacement candidates have been elected after six officials were removed from office with less than 50% of the vote. In California recall elections, the candidate who receives the most votes wins, unlike in a special election, where a candidate must win a majority.
This creates a conundrum of a recalled official garnering more voter support than the replacement candidate who “wins” the recall.
In the 2018 recall of former stateSen. Josh Newman, for instance, (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article145349124.html) his replacement, Republican Ling Ling Chang, came out on top with just under 34% of the vote. Newman points out that he had more votes in his favor; nearly 42% of voters opposed his recall.
“So I got more votes by way of ‘no, don’t kick him out,’ than she got by ‘yes, please put her in,’” Newman said.
Newman won back his Senate seat in the next regular election and then went on to write Prop. 5 (https://www.kcra.com/article/california-voters-prop-5-changes-recall-election-process/73175034).
One of the proposition’s most outspoken opponents is Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a former talk radio host who pushed for Newman’s recall in 2017.
How Prop. 5 opponents feel
DeMaio sees Prop. 5 as an attempt by the ruling party to evade recalls. “What they want to do is create a situation where politicians trying to fend off a recall can say, ‘Don’t vote for the recall or else you won’t be represented for 12 months. You’ll lose your voice,’” he told us.
Actually, Article II, Section 15 of the California Constitution, says a recall election must be held within 60 and 80 days of recall petition signatures being certified. The election may be held within 180 days of certification if it is consolidated with the next regularly scheduled election.
Arguments against Prop. 5 ignore that the current system created instances where replacement candidates got elected with less than 50% of the vote.
They decry the cost of conducting special elections and oppose that Prop. 5 would allow a recalled official to run in a special election to fill the vacancy.
There have been 182 attempts (https://www.sos.ca.gov/elections/recalls/recall-history-california-1913-present) to recall state officials in California. Eleven of those made the ballot, and only six were successful.
Some view the current recall system as “a weapon for political operators (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5.pdf) to undo election results they don’t like,” to quote the League of Women Voters and others.
Prop. 5 cannot put an end to the political gamesmanship, but it can safeguard the will of the voters by following the principle of majority rule.
McClatchy Media’s California editorial board strongly urges a “yes” vote on Proposition 5.

7. The Lt. Gov is independently elected statewide, so succession has democratic legitimacy.

4. Motivation: incumbent/political protection; author Josh Newman was recalled in 2018.
5. The Lt. Gov as automatic successor may not reflect voters' desire for change.
6. Endorsed by: CA GOP, HJTA, Reform California (Carl DeMaio), Election Integrity Project; editorial boards: SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, SCNG (OC Register, LA Daily News, Press-Telegram), San Diego Union-Tribune, Santa Cruz Sentinel.

The reform is modest and coherent: it doesn't touch the recall power itself. Californians retain exactly the same ability to remove an official — the same signature thresholds, same timing, same yes/no vote. The "takes away your right to choose" argument cuts less deeply than it sounds, because in the most important case (Governor), the replacement is the Lt. Gov — someone Californians elected statewide. And if the recall happens early in a term, voters choose a new Governor at the next statewide election anyway. For legislators, voters still choose — via special election. The only case where voters don't directly choose is other constitutional officers, where the Governor appoints — but that's identical to what happens today when such an office is vacated by death or resignation, and those appointments are subject to... well, the appointee serves until the next election (for constitutional officers, appointment until next election where the office is filled). Hmm, actually for statewide offices other than Governor/Lt. Gov, the appointee serves the remainder of the term I believe. Let me think about that. Actually, for state offices elected statewide, the Governor's appointee serves the balance of the term. But regardless, this mirrors existing vacancy law, which voters have long accepted.

The strongest argument against — the recalled official being able to run in the special election to fill their own seat — is indeed odd, but it's not disqualifying in my judgment. It preserves voter choice (voters can reject the recalled official); it simply eliminates the current irrationality where an official who is recalled in June can't run in the special election in November but can run in the regular election two years later. The unlimited recall-fundraising concern is real but narrow (state law already restricts use of recall funds). And it's worth noting that under the current system, the "runner-up" dynamics are worse: a candidate with 28% support takes over immediately with no further recourse.

The cost argument cuts both ways (LAO says unknown net effect — savings in some scenarios, costs in others, and these events are rare — 6 successful recalls in 110+ years).

The "incumbent protection" argument has some political truth (Democrats dominate Sacramento and would benefit in the near term), but the principle applies symmetrically: if a Republican official were recalled in the future, the same rules would apply. The deeper point is that recalls shouldn't be a mechanism for the out-of-power party to seize an office via a low-turnout plurality race — if they want the office, they should win a regular election. Removing an unfit official remains fully possible, and arguably more likely to succeed because voters won't be distracted by/afraid of the successor question.

Majority-rule principle, good-government group support (LWV, Common Cause — organizations with long histories of supporting voter empowerment), the Secretary of State's backing, alignment with most other states and existing vacancy law, and preserving the recall itself — these make the case for YES stronger overall. The opposition is largely partisan-Republican opposition mixed with the Chronicle's single-provision objection, which — while legitimate — is outweighed by the core reform's merits.

So my answer: YES.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Election of State Officials. The State Constitution establishes legislative, executive, and judicial state offices. Some state officials represent parts of the state, known as districts. Other state officials, like the Governor or Attorney General, represent the entire state. Voters elect people to represent them in state offices for set terms. For example, a state Assembly Member is elected to a two-year term and the Governor is elected to a four-year term. To run for a state office, candidates must submit specific nomination documents before the election. State law sets when this “nomination period” occurs.
Recall of State Officials. The State Constitution allows voters to remove state officials from office before their term ends through a recall. A recall is an election in which voters are asked whether to remove an official from office. To qualify a recall for the ballot, supporters of the recall must collect a certain number of signatures from the official’s district (or statewide for statewide offices). Since 1913, 11 state recall efforts have qualified for the ballot (nine legislators and two Governors) and six have resulted in an official’s removal from office (five legislators and one Governor).
Two Questions in Recall Elections. In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office. The number of candidates appearing in the second question varies. For example, there were 135 candidates in the 2003 Governor recall election and 46 candidates in the 2021 Governor recall election. If a state official is recalled, the person who receives the most votes in the second question assumes the office.
Vacant State Offices. State officials may leave office before the end of their term for reasons other than a recall. For example, they may die or resign. When this happens, the office becomes vacant. The process to fill a vacant office varies by office. Typically, a vacant seat in the Assembly or Senate is filled through a special election called by the Governor. The Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor when there is a vacancy in the office of the Governor. Vacancies in other executive offices (for example, the Lieutenant Governor or Attorney General) and the Supreme Court and Courts of Appeal are filled by appointments by the Governor.
Frequency of Elections. Statewide elections in California are scheduled every two years. In scheduled election years, a primary election is held in either March or June, depending on the year, and a general election is held in November. In addition to scheduled elections, the state and local governments may call special elections to address specific issues. For example, the Governor may call a special election to fill a vacant Assembly seat.
Elections Administration in California. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have election-related workload. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
Paying for State Recall Elections. State law requires the California Department of Finance to work with state and local elections officials to estimate the cost of a recall election for a state office. The department is required to send the estimate to the Legislature. The Legislature reviews the estimate and may provide funding for the election. Any remaining costs are paid by the Secretary of State’s and counties’ budgets.
PROPOSAL
As described below, Proposition 5 changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.
Removes Second Question From Recall Elections. Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election. This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices. If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant. Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office. In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election. The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
Creates Separate Process for Filling the Office of the Governor. The process for filling the office of the Governor depends on when the recall occurs. If the Governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, Proposition 5 says that the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election. If the Governor is recalled later in the term, the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor for the rest of the term.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Fiscal Effects Depend on Frequency of Recalls and the Offices Recalled. Whether there would be costs or savings compared with today depends on the frequency of future recalls and the offices recalled. A recall of a statewide office (for example, Lieutenant Governor) would affect state elections officials and local elections officials in all 58 counties. A recall of a district-based office (for example, a state Senator or Assembly Member) would only affect state elections officials and local elections officials in those districts.
Potential Costs. Proposition 5 could result in higher costs associated with future recall elections if a special election is necessary to fill the vacant office after a recall. For example, a legislative office made vacant after a recall typically would be filled through a special election. If that special election could not be consolidated with a scheduled election, elections officials would need to run a standalone special election. The cost to state and local elections officials to administer such a special election could be millions of dollars per election.
Potential Savings. Proposition 5 could result in lower costs by removing the second question from the ballot. These savings would occur when a Governor is recalled in the latter part of the term and for other offices where vacancies are filled by appointment. There would be savings because ballots and voting materials would no longer include information about replacement candidates. The amount of savings would depend on how many candidates there would have been on the ballot if the second question remained but could be millions of dollars per election.
Net Effect Depends on Circumstances of Future Recall Efforts. The net fiscal effect is unknown because it depends on future recall elections. Proposition 5 could lead to savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars to administer recall elections. How these savings or costs would be shared by state and county governments would depend on future decisions by the Legislature. This net fiscal effect represents less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
California’s recall process should protect our democracy by allowing for the removal of an elected official who is corrupt or abusing their power. It should never be used as a tactic to ‘redo’ an election as a political or partisan scheme. Proposition 5 will restore the recall to its original purpose by making it fair, democratic, and accountable to the will of the majority.
Under current law, a statewide recall ballot asks voters two questions in sequence:
(1) Should the official be recalled? (2) If so, who should replace them?
By being connected, these two questions create a dangerous loophole. An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election. This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this play out in the 2021 gubernatorial recall. Voters rejected it decisively. The recall lost by nearly the same number of votes that the Governor won the regular election with. But California taxpayers were forced to spend more than $200 million on an election whose outcome simply reconfirmed what voters had already decided. Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money. And had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with support from only about 28% of all recall voters.
Proposition 5 makes a single, commonsense change: it removes the second question from the recall ballot .
Under Prop. 5, in a state-level recall, voters would decide one very simple and important question: whether an officeholder should be removed. If a majority votes yes, that office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor and if the recall occurs early enough, voters would elect a replacement at the next statewide election; other statewide officers would be filled by appointment under existing rules; legislative seats by special election. No shortcuts, no loopholes, and no replacement candidate winning office without majority voter support.
In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election, not a same-day replacement contest.
By eliminating the second question, Proposition 5 removes the incentive and ability to weaponize recalls as a shortcut for partisan advantage. Recalls could not be gamed to overturn the results of regular elections or install candidates who couldn’t win under normal conditions.
The framers of our recall process intended to safeguard voters against corrupt and unaccountable officials, not to provide a weapon for political operators to undo election results they don’t like. Proposition 5 preserves the recall as a tool for accountability while preventing it from being used to sidestep regular elections and majority rule.
Vote YES on Proposition 5 to protect majority rule, defend taxpayers, and restore California’s recall process back to the voters it was designed to serve.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
California Fair Political Practices Commission
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
Disregard the mental gymnastics the other side is doing here to tie us in knots and try to make sense of the truly nonsensical.
They say Proposition 5 “protects democracy.” It does the opposite-it erodes one of the fundamental elements of our recall process: to choose who replaces the recalled politician.
That’s not protecting democracy-that’s protecting political elites.
They call California’s system a “dangerous loophole.” It’s worked for 100 years, ousting politicians who abuse their office and replacing them with whoever the voters decide will do better.
Proposition 5 would create a loophole, not close one. The other side is gaslighting you. They think you won’t notice. Don’t be fooled.
If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises.
Now, he wants to burn it down on his way out the door-making future recalls less effective and keeping politicians like him less accountable.
If you traded in your car, would you want to know what you were getting in return-or would you be happy to sign it away and let the salesman stick you in a jalopy of their choosing after you’ve already committed? That’s what Proposition 5 asks you to do.
Our recall system will continue to work just fine, if we don’t let political elites with sour grapes tinker with it to their benefit.
Vote NO!
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 will take away your voice and erode your ability to remove and replace failed or corrupt politicians from office.
California politicians already have too much power. Proposition 5 gives them even more-and it does it by taking power away from you, the voters.
For over 100 years, California’s recall process has given us the ability to remove elected officials who abuse their office, break promises or fail to do the job they were elected to do. And, when that happens, the current process allows you-not politicians-to choose who replaces them.
Proposition 5 changes that system forever and takes power away from the people.
Today, a recall election asks two simple questions: Should the elected official be removed from office? If so, who should replace them? That means Californians can remove a failed politician and immediately choose someone new to take their place.
Proposition 5 keeps the first part but eliminates your ability to vote for a replacement.
Instead, Sacramento political insiders would decide what happens next. In many cases, politicians themselves-not voters-would choose who fills the vacancy, essentially allowing them to appoint another one of their friends or political allies to replace the one you just ousted.
In other cases, rather than an immediate replacement, the seat would sit vacant until another costly election-funded by you, the taxpayer-was scheduled months later. And here’s the kicker; that failed politician you just ran out the door for failure or corruption, they'd be allowed to run in that next election to regain control of the seat they just lost.
In either case, your vote matters less, and the political establishment gains more control.
Californians deserve the right to remove an elected official-and to choose who comes next. Proposition 5 takes away half of that right, and that’s wrong.
Supporters claim this measure improves democracy. It doesn’t. Democracy means voters-not Sacramento politicians-get to choose their leaders, when to give them the boot and who to replace them with. Proposition 5 undermines that fundamental concept.
Ask yourself: if you vote to remove a governor or another statewide elected official, shouldn’t you also decide who replaces them?
The answer is clear.
It’s also worth wondering why this measure is on the ballot in the first place. Why fix a system that isn’t broken and has been working just fine for over a century?
Well, the author of this proposal himself was recalled by California voters when he voted to raise gas taxes after promising not to. Instead of respecting the will of the people, he now wants to rewrite the rules and protect politicians like him from any meaningful accountability. California’s recall belongs to the people-not politicians. Protect your voice. Protect your vote. Protect your right to hold elected officials accountable.
Vote NO on Proposition 5.
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 5
Don’t be misled. Proposition 5 preserves your power to recall an official by majority vote while closing the loophole that allows a replacement candidate to take office with a small fraction of the vote.
Under current law, voters decide whether to remove an official by majority vote, but the replacement can win with far less than a majority. In 2021, a replacement candidate could have become Governor with support from 28% of recall voters. That is not majority rule.
Opponents want you to believe Proposition 5 takes away your right to choose. It does not. The real question is whether someone should become Governor with support from only a small fraction of California voters.
Proposition 5 preserves the recall while separating the decision to remove an officeholder from the decision about who should serve next. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor-elected statewide by California voters-provides continuity of government until voters choose the next Governor through a regular election. Voters will still choose their elected officials. But candidates seeking statewide office should earn that office in a regular election based on their qualifications, record, and plans for California, not use a recall as a shortcut to power.
A recall should decide whether an officeholder remains in office. Choosing who governs should happen in a regular election, where candidates earn the support of California voters. Proposition 5 protects the recall, respects majority rule, and ensures candidates run on their own merits. Vote YES on Proposition 5.

Now I have a good understanding of the proposition. It's SCA 1 (Chapter 204, Statutes of 2024) by Senator Josh Newman. It changes the recall process for state officers:

1. Removes the second question (who replaces the recalled official) from recall ballots
2. If Governor is recalled, Lt. Governor becomes Governor for remainder of term or until successor is elected (if recall occurs early in the term)
3. For other recalled officers, office remains vacant until filled by special election or appointment per existing law
4. A recalled officer may run in the special election to fill the office

Supporters: League of Women Voters of California, California Common Cause, Dan Schnur (former FPPC chair). The main proponent is Josh Newman (who was recalled in 2018 after voting for the gas tax increase, then re-elected in 2020).

Opponents: Senate Minority Leader Brian W. Jones, Assemblymember Joe Patterson (Republicans).

Key considerations for analysis:

Pro:
- Closes the loophole where a replacement can win with a small fraction of the vote (e.g., in 2021, Larry Elder could have won with ~28% of voters' support while Newsom had 60%+ support in the recall question)
- Reduces incentive for partisan recall attempts to "redo" elections
- Aligns California with most other states where recalls fill vacancies via succession or separate elections
- Prevents the "kangaroo" scenario where a recalled official could theoretically run and win in their own replacement race (actually, under Prop 5, the recalled officer CAN be a candidate in the special election)
- Saves potentially millions in election administration costs in some scenarios

Con:
- Takes away voters' right to choose replacement immediately
- Vacancy filled by appointment (Governor appoints for other statewide offices) - "political insiders" choose
- For legislative offices, an additional costly special election, leaving the office vacant for months
- The recalled official could run again in the special election to fill the vacancy
- Seen as incumbent protection / motivated by Josh Newman's own recall experience

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.

Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.

Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.

Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”
